rv.q: This is an impressive staging, peppered with sensationally unhinged performances, not all of them from Coogan.
This classic Cold War farce feels more timely and more terrifying than ever.

This production achieves the dubious feat of turning an edgy, absurdist story into broad entertainment with accessible laughs, along with a few topical references and excellent performances all round.
It’s an accomplished, funny West End comedy, and even if the Cold War is over it still has some topical bite.
What it lacks is any fresh theatrical reinvention of the story for the stage - or any cutting edge.
Perhaps it’s that framework that makes this something of a hit-and-miss evening.
It’s a lovable but overly reverential approach to a film classic that’s sturdy enough to withstand a braver spin.

It also made you wish the show’s co-adaptors, Armando Iannucci and Sean Foley, had applied a few more creative flourishes to what is, all in all, a stolid remake of the classic Stanley Kubrick Cold War satire.
It’s a question the show never adequately answers, trapped between the film’s formidable legacy and an inability to recreate it anew theatrically.
Sean Foley, alas, is no Stanley Kubrick.
The rest of us can delight in a masterful recreation of sublime comic acting, even if we do wince at the show's largely unmitigated, and depressingly relentless, raw misogyny.
Happily, Armando Iannucci and Sean Foley’s explosively funny new stage adaptation also pulls off that near-impossible high-wire act.

Coogan has a ball being funny as the languid, posh RAF man with a vocabulary beyond US generals, the bland ineffectual President, the gung-ho pilot riding an atom bomb like a rodeo bronco and especially as former Nazi Strangelove.
Most of the supporting cast add little more than fluff and distraction for Coogan’s costume/character changes.
It may be doable but that doesn’t make it worth doing.
It’s entertaining but never quite as savage as you expect.
This is then – rather like Dr Strangelove with his rebellious prosthetic limbs – an evening of different parts, some functioning better than others.
Without a doubt, it’s Coogan’s talent that makes the show a success.
I came out of the theatre still smiling from the brilliance of this mind-blowing production.
It's Coogan's triumph and he finally lays the ghost of the tiresome (for me, anyway) Alan Partridge.
Yet Coogan is priceless. The black-gloved pneumatic hand that keeps betraying Strangelove's past by rising to a Nazi salute is very funny.
The show is great fun and super-slick, but lacks the genuine chill of the film – it’s a bit too entertaining for its own good.

cn.t: Critics praise Steve Coogan's virtuosic multi-role performance in this faithful stage adaptation of Kubrick's classic, though many question whether the reverent, film-faithful approach justifies transferring the cinematic masterpiece to theatre.
